not hang on to the word ' annihilate '; it was improvidently used; I did not mean that. We could put it out of existence so far as being a corporation with powers from this Parliament is concerned, and let it merge into the other.

The hon. gentleman
will agree with me when I state it this way:	If we once erect a company ;nto
the status of a Dominion company it must, after that, read its powers under our Railway Act; so in the case of a railway company it must interpret its corporate powers under the general Railway Act of Canada. If we once take that step either by original legislation here incorporating companies or by declaring a company, incorporated provincially, to be for the general advantage of Canada, then we never more can reverse the operation and" make it read its corporate powers in the light of a provincial general Act or in the light of a provincial special Act.

Except as I have
stated, I think.

We could, of course,
after giving it certain powers by Dominion legislation, curtail or abrogate those powers; but we could never bring it under the jurisdiction of an Act of the province as opposed to the general jurisdiction of an Act of the Dominion, nor could we, if I am right, once we have declared a provincial company to be for the general advantage of Canada, ever afterwards degrade the company, if I may use the term, or turn it back under the jurisdiction of a provincial legislature.

Does my hon. friend contend that under the clauses of the Act you can take jurisdiction over a company? I do not read the Act in this way. We can not take jurisdiction over a company and transform a provincial company into a federal. Our jurisdiction is to control the company, a different proposition.

It goes further. Section 6 of the Railway Act, read in the light of decision of the Privy Council in the Bell Telephone case, will convince my hon. friend that the law goes further than that, that not only that the company's works and undertakings are under the jurisdiction of the Dominion, but it must read its corporate powers from our Railway Act, or from our general Act, or from our special Act, as the ease may be, and no longer read its corporate powers as a company from any provincial Act.

I admit that the moment we have declared the work created by a provincial company to be for the general advantage of Canada, as we have clearly the power to do, all the powers which have created that work certainly come under our jurisdiction and we become paramount to that extent.

And the company comes under our jurisdiction to that extent. That being the case, the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) would fail to meet its end. It is subject to a still additional objection. If it were passed in that form, there would doubtless

come the question later on as to whether the road was completed or not, whether it was constructed or not, and there is a sense in which a road is never constructed. If a mile remained to be built, or if the legislature added to the charter power to add another ten miles, the effect might be that the road could never come under the jurisdiction of this Parliament. Consequently, whatever may be done in the way of meeting the wishes of the province in this regard will have to be done in such a way that the Governor in Council shall have power to bring the railways under the operation of the Eailway Act, to bring them within the system of making them Dominion companies at such time as shall be defined generally; but in such a way that it shall be within the power of the Governor in Council to declare at will that the time has arrived.
I propose, in the absence of the First Minister, to substitute another wording for clause 15. Perhaps the amendment of the hon. member had better be disposed of first. I am quite aware that a great deal can be said in favour of the jurisdiction of the province being preserved while the road is under construction. Under the circumstances stated by the hon. member for Edmonton, namely that the construction of the road is being provided for out of funds guaranteed by these provinces or out of subsidies given by them in whole or to a great extent, no particular object, at all events I think no sufficient object, would be served by taking them under our jurisdiction until the roads are ready for operation.

My hon. friend has expressed his disapproval of the amendment I have had the honour to offer, in points of detail but not in points of principle. He admits that it is right and proper that the province should have control during construction, but he says that it is not possible under the terms of my amendment. I am compelled to say that he has by no means convinced me, so far as his argument has gone, that the terms of my amendment are outside that which is fair and right or outside the possibility of working practicability or outside the limits of the constitution. Of course, I cannot force my views upon the House and I do not intend to spend any great length of time in attempting to do so, but I may say that my hon. friend has not offered what appears to me to be any convincing argument against the Government adopting the principle that I have put forward in such terms as may be

apt and within the limits of the constitution. If a thing is right it is the business of the Government, in making an Act, to make provision to meet that which is right when it has been brought to their attention. In regard to my hon. friend's suggestion, I find just as much fault -with his amendment as he finds with mine. If I understand it in one way, I find fault with it; and if I understand it in another way, I am perfectly satisfied with it. But I shall have to ask my hon. friend just how it is to be interpreted. When he speaks of the 'works and undertaking ' of the Canadian Northern Western Company, does he desire to express the measure of those lines that are now under guarantee, or does he desire to express the limit of the lines that are under charter?

The term ' works and undertaking ' has been interpreted in the courts more than once, and has a well defined legal meaning. If the company adds to its line in any way in the future, then that addition would immediately come under the words ' works and undertaking.'

Take the line chartered
from Edmonton to the boundary of the province, a distance say of about three hundred and fifty miles. Under the terms of my hon. friend's proposal, would it be possible to declare the works of the Canadian Northern Western Railway Company works for the general advantage of Canada before that line was completed to the boundary of the province?
Yes. As far as the possibility is concerned we could pass this today and declare the whole line for the advantage of Canada to-morrow.

There are 66.31 miles of
the Canadian Northwestern Railway Company under provincial guarantee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Consisting of different
lines in different parts of the province, but all under one charter?

Yes, but having no physical connection except through the Canadian Northern Railway system. Am I
5 p.m. to understand that this proposal means that subsection 5 will not be brought into effect until the whole of these guaranteed lines have been completed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the situation is a very plain one. The only difficulty that arises is that the power of making the

declaration under the British , North America Act is invested with certain limitations. My hon. friend says that there is a provincial charter which embraces a number of roads not physically connected wiHh each other but all connected1 with the Canadian Northern railway system. I do not wish to trench upon provincial jurisdiction in any way except so far as may be absolutely essential for the working out of this arrangement. As 1 understand it, the desire of the provincial autnoriues is that during construction those roads shall not !be brought under federal jurisdiction, but that immediately after operation begins they shall be brought undOT federal jurisdiction.	The difficulty that
presents itself is this: Inasmuch as those roads are all embraced within one charter we do not conceive that it is possible to make the provision which my hon. friend suggests for the reason that it is' not competent for this Parliament under the British North America Act to say that irpm time to time a certain part of the undertaking of a company shall be subject to federal jurisdiction.	We do not understand that that is possible. We are ready to proceed either in one way or the other. We are ready to say that these roads shall 'be brought under federal jurisdiction at once during the period of construction or that they shall not be brought under federal jurisdiction until they have all been completed. One of these roads may be completed while others remain in course of construction, and in that case, according to the terms of this amendment, the Governor in Council could not under this statutory provision make the declaration until the whole had been completed; and, therefore, it would involve the disadvantage-1 am speaking from the provincial point, oi view-of keeping out of federal jurisdiction those roads which had been constructed till the rest were completed. Therefore, we have to deal with it in one or other of these ways, and I understand the wish and desire of the provinicai authorities is- that we should deal with it in this way. The third method which my hon. friend suggests and would like to see carried out is impracticable on account of constitutional limitations. However, I think there would be a remedy for the situation by the combined action in the future of the provincial legislature and this Parliament. I think that by action of the provincial legislature it would be 287
possible to select one of those roads which had been completed, and transfer it to another company for purposes of operation, and then for this Parliament to declare the undertaking of that company subject to the jurisdiction of the lederai Parliament and the Board of Kailway Commissioners.
Do I understand that the amendment suggested by the Solicitor General meets with the approval of the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

I have not got it clear in my mind yet whether it is intended to make the declaration upon the completion of the lines so far as they have been guaranteed, or upon the completion of the lines so far as they have been chartered. I take it that it is not the intention to make the declaration until the lines have been completed as far as they have been guaranteed. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Guaranteed by the provincial governments?

There are, with respect to all of these lines, 663 miles guaranteed, and all of these lines are more or less under construction. Is it proposed to make the declaration that these are works for the general advantage of Canada, as soon as the 663 miles are completed, or is it intended to make it before they are completed, or is it intended to defer the declaration until the lines, as far as they have been chartered, are completed?

There is no difference of opinion, in so far as I have been able to find out from the representatives of the provincial governments, between the provincial governments and this Government as to the intended time of declaring these works respectively to be for the general advantage of 'Canada. At the same time, it is impossible to put into words anything that will place specific limitations upon the power of this Parliament. We have reserved to Parliament the power to declare the works and undertakings of the Canadian Northern Western, say, to be for the general advantage of Canada, although possibly one or more or all of the branches may not be completed. Otherwise, the intention, neither of the provincial governments nor of this Government, would be carried out. There might be, for example, 600 miles in operation and one or two other branches which had not been



started. We have reserved the right to declare them to be for the general advantage of Canada, when in the opinion of the Governor in Council, such a substantial portion of the line is ready for operation as to make the declaration a carrying out of the spirit of this provision.
This is a very extraordinary power which is usually exercised by Parliament alone. Is there a precedent for the delegation of this power to the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is not a delegation; Parliament makes the declaration and leaves the date of the declaration to be fixed by the Governor in Council.
I understand that but it is the act of the Governor in Council that declares this particular work to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.

No, all that the Governor in Council declares is that the railway is constructed and is open for operation. This Parliament declares that the work is an undertaking for the general advantage of Canada but postpones the proclamation of it until a time fixed by the Governor in Council.

My hon. friend from
Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) asks if there is a precedent for such an amendment as the one provided by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). In so far as my knowledge of this matter goes, the objections raised by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) are entirely imaginary. We have the precedent which my hon. friend asks for in the case of the province of Manitoba. In that province we experienced all the conditions in respect to the construction of branch lines years ago and every branch line that was guaranteed by the province, or which was undertaken to be constructed under .a pro-, vincial charter, was immediately declared by this Parliament to be a work for the general advantage of Canada and amalgamated with the Canadian Northern. My hon. friend speaks of the jurisdiction of the provinces, control of the Railway Commission in respect to traffic, of the enterprise being under the control of the province during construction and of making orders for location. All these conditions were imposed by this Parliament in the construction of the 'Manitoba lines of railway from 1901 on until to-day. Not only

did this Parliament declare every branch line that bad been guaranteed, iand that was built with the money of that province to be for the general benefit of. Canada, but in the legislation, as it was going through each year, a clause was added stating:
That before commencing the construction of the lines above mentioned the location thereof shall first be approved by the Governor in Council.
It wias under these restrictions, as my hon. friend would call them now, that all the lines in Manitoba were constructed and I do not think, there is anything at all 'in his suggestion that this Parliament is undertaking to restrict in any way the jurisdiction of the western provinces. On the contrary, I think that my hon. friend the Solicitor General has gone entirely too far in the proposal which he is making and I do not believe it is necessary. We did not find it necessary in our undertakings, when, as a member of the Government of the province of Manitoba, I was assisting in securing the construction of those lines. No conflict of interest arose and I do not anticipate that any conflict of interest will arise between the provinces and the Dominion in the present case. Therefore, I regard, the objections raised by the hon. member for Edmonton as being entirely imaginary and I do not think there is any necessity for the amendment as proposed on either side of the House in respect to the matter or as affecting the conditions under which we can secure branch lines to be built in any province in Canada.

While we are interested in the reminiscences of my hon. friend (Mr. Rogers), still they are not valuable in this connection. There are railway companies under construction in the province of Alberta, and we are dealing with railway companies which are chartered by the province and not by the Dominion.
Ours were the same.

Some of them were and some of them were not. There are railways being constructed in Alberta under the Canadian Northern charter and which are being aided by the provincial Government, lines to the length of 774 miles, and aided by guarantees to the amount of $11,000,000. These lines are under the jurisdiction of this Parliament and of the Railway Commission, and we are not bringing them into the question at all. But

in regard to the lines that are chartered by the province, aided entirely by the province, whatever may have been the experience in Manitoba is not to the point. The point is that we want to have the control of the results of the expenditure of our own money, so far as the accommodation of the people is concerned. If the relations between the Canadian Northern railway and the Government of Manitoba were such that satisfactory arrangements were always made in that province, it does not follow that the same conditions would prevail in other provinces. Certain things are right, and when they are right they are generally expedient, and the provincial Governments which have accepted such enormous financial responsibility on behalf of their people in order to secure railway advantages are entitled to all the measure of protection this Government can give them. The position stated by the Solicitor General and the Prime Minister simply amounts to this: we will consider the position of the provinces, and we will deal with that situation as we please under the terms of the Act. That is not very satisfactory, nor do I think it is compelled by a constitutional limitation. I am not a constitutional authority, I admit, but when I read the plain English of the British North America Act I find this:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the Parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada.
That is to say, the declaration may be made after completion as well as before completion. On the plain reading of the Act, it is certainly contemplated that works may be declared to be for the general advantage of Canada after they are completed, and I take it for granted they may be declared to be for the general advantage of Canada after they are completed, without declaring them to be for the general advantage of Canada before they are completed. Or this Parliament may declare a completed work to be for the general advantage of Canada when it would not so desire to declare an uncompleted work. I believe that my amendment is fair, and reasonable, and right, and if my object cannot be obtained in the form in which I have placed it before the House, there surely must be some other means of arriving at what is such an eminently fair and reasonable proposition. When a fair and reasonable proposition is placed before the Govern-287J
ment, and its fairness and reasonableness have to be admitted, if the Government is not able to accept that proposition it is their business to find a way by which what is fair and right can be embodied in the statutes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is perfectly true that
work can be declared, either before or after its completion, but the difficulty we find is that the proposal of my hon. friend would involve the possession by this Parliament of the power to declare that each mile of the road as it was completed should become a work for the general advantage of Canada. We do not think that this Parliament possesses that power. Therefore we have left the matter in such shape that the road during construction shall remain under the control of the provincial legislature.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With the consent of the House, may I be permitted to read some telegrams which have been sent respecting the appalling disaster to which reference was made in the House yesterday ?
The following is a telegram from His Majesty to His Royal Highness the Governor General:
London, 30th May, 1914.
I am deeply grieved at the awful disaster to the Empress of Ireland in which alas so many Canadians have lost their lives. The Queen and I assure you of our heartfelt sympathy with those who mourn for the loss of their relatives and friends.
(Sgd) George R.I.
A telegram from Queen Alexandra to His Royal Highness the Governor General:
London, May 30, 1914.
The terrible disaster that has occurred to the Atlantic liner, Empress of Ireland, in the St. Lawrence river grieves me more than I can say. Up to last night we had hoped in London that most if not all the lives had been saved, but this morning I learn that the first report was too true and that over 1,000 people had been drowned. I wish to express to you my intense sorrow in this awful catastrophe and beg of you kindly to see that my heartfelt sympathy may be conveyed to the relatives of all those who have perished.
(Sgd) Alexandra.
A telegram from the right hon. the Secretary of State for the Colonies to His Royal Highness the Governor General:
London, 29th May, 1914.
Governor General,
Ottawa.
I have learned with the deepest regret of wreck of ss. Empress of Ireland and the disastrous loss of life which has occurred. Please take what steps as are possible to make known my sympathy with relatives in Canada of those who have perished.
(Sgd) Ilarccurt.
His Royal Highness the Governor General sent me the following telegram on the 29th instant:
Toronto, May 29, 1914.
Borden,
Ottawa, Ont.
On behalf of the Duchess and myself I desire to express to you our deep grief at the terrible disaster to the Empress of Ireland and our heartfelt sympathy with the families of those who have perished.
(Sgd) Arthur.
The following message has been transmitted through the office of the High Commissioner from His Serene Highness Prince Alexander of Teck:
Right Hon. R. L. Borden.
Have now received the following message from Prince Alexander of Teck:

' Grieved to hear of disaster Empress of Ireland. Kindly convey sympathy of Princess and myself with relatives of victims.
(Sgd) Teck.*
A telegram from the Prime Minister of New Zealand:
Dunedin, May 29, 1914.
Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
On behalf of Government and people of New Zealand desire express sincere sympathy with our sister dominion in appalling loss of life which has taken place in the foundering Empress of Ireland and our heartfelt condolence with relatives and friends of those who have perished.
(Sgd) Massey, Prime Minister.
To which the following reply has been sent:
Ottawa, 30th May, 1914.
Prime Minister,
Dunedin, New Zealand.
On behalf of Government and people of Canada I send our deep and sincere appreciation of your message and our profound sympathy for those in your dominion who have been bereaved by the loss of relatives and friends in this appalling disaster.
(Sgd) Borden.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 5.37 p.m.
Monday, June 1, 1914.
